Anatomy And Imaging Indications. The Normal Breast

Anca Ciurea, Ioana Ben

30.1. Anatomy and physiology of the breast

The breasts are specialized modifified skin appendages, defifining the features of class Mammalia. They are located on the anterior thoracic wall, between the second and sixth ribs and from the midaxillary line to the lateral border of the sternum. A smaller part of the mammary gland extends toward the axilla, forming the axillary tail of Spence. The axillary tail is important because breast cancer can also develop in this breast region; it must be included in all breast examinations.

The breasts are attached to the skin and fascia of major and minor pectoralis muscles by the ligaments of Cooper (condensations of connective fifibrous tissue). They are covered by adipose tissue and skin.

In the central part of the breast is the nipple, surrounded by the areola and, together, they form the nipple areolar complex.

The breast comprises 15-20 breast lobules, triangularly shaped (base towards the periphery and tip towards the nipple). Each lobule is centered by a lactiferous duct that opens into the nipple. The lactiferous ducts are progressively branching and end in the ne milk-secreting alveoli (small hollow spaces), arranged in grape-like clusters.

The arterial supply of the breast is provided mainly by branches derived from the internal thoracic artery and the axillary artery, while the venous drainage is mainly to the axillary vein.

The lymphatic drainage of the breast is mainly to the axillary lymph nodes and the parasternal lymph nodes. Lymphatic drainage is essential because of its role in the metastasis of cancer cells. Imaging of patients with suspicious breast lesions should always include the axilla and the parasternal region for accurate staging and treatment.

During the reproductive life cycle, the breasts demonstrate morphologic alteration. During puberty, the breasts enlarge due to glandular development and fat deposition.

There are also changes during the menstrual cycle. In the luteal or secretory phase of the cycle, the lobules become larger, the alveoli increase in number, and there is associated edema in the adipose and connective tissue. In this period, the breasts may enlarge (including the axillary tail) and become painful.

New glandular tissue forms during pregnancy and lactation, and the breasts

At menopause, due to the reduction of estrogen and progesterone levels, there is a progressive involution and atrophy of all the structures: ducts, alveoli, connective and adipose tissue. Hormone replacement therapy diminishes these changes and may even stimulate proliferative changes.

The physiological changes reflflect in the imaging appearance of the breast, which is different from person to person or at the same person, depending on the age and physiological status. In other words, depending on the age, physiological status or clinical complaints, the indications and the performance of the different imaging methods used to evaluate the breast are different.

30.2. Imaging techniques

30.2.1. Mammography is a technique that uses x-rays to image the breast. The x-rays generated by the mammography machine are based upon a molybdenum or rhodium anode (not on tungsten anode, like other x-rays machines). They are ideal for imaging soft tissues from the breast (glandular, connective, and adipose tissues).

Images are acquired in two standard views, mediolateral oblique (MLO) and cranio-caudal (CC) (fifigure 238). Contrary to other body parts in which two perpendicular views are acquired, the MLO view is performed in the breast instead of the lateral view because, in the MLO projection, the axillary tail is also visualized.

During mammography, the breast is compressed by a plastic compression paddle to minimize the breast thickness and to spread the breast tissue evenly, hence reducing the radiation dose.

Tomosynthesis (or 3D mammography) is a technique in which multiple sections are obtained in the same projection, at different angles, with the tube moving continuously on an arch. The images are then reconstructed in thin slices (1 mm), which will allow better visualization of the lesions by eliminating the superimposing of the breast tissue (fifigure 239).

Contrast-enhanced spectral mammo -

graphy (CESM) is a technique that combines mammography with the intravenous administration of iodinated contrast media. Two images are acquired, in quick succession, with two different energies of the x-ray beam. The obtained images are then subtracted with the cancellation of the background noise of the breast parenchyma. On the substracted images, only the iodine uptaken by the lesions is visible (fifigure 240).

30.2.2. Ultrasound is performed with linear, high-frequency transducers that allow optimal visualization of superfificial structures. The differential diagnosis of the breast masses is based on the morphological characteristics depicted on greyscale ultrasound. Doppler ultrasound and elastography can offer supplementary information and aid in differential diagnosis. However, they are never used alone in the fifinal assessment of breast lesions, only in correlation with the 2D ultrasound (fifigure 241).

30.2.3. Breast MRI is the most sensitive imaging method in breast examination because it overcomes the masking effect of the breast tissue. For the evaluation of implants in the augmented breast, particular sequences visualize the implant-related pathology without the administration of contrast media (fifigure 242). 30.3. Indications and limits of breast imaging methods

30.3.1. Mammography: Indications:

  • screening method in women over< the age of 40. In most European countries, the screening programs include women between the ages of 50 and 73 and the screening mammography is performed every two years. The screening programs allow breast cancer diagnosis in early stages, with a consecutive signifificant reduction in the number of deaths caused by the disease.

30.4. The normal breast

30.4.1. Mammography

The adipose tissue appears lucent on mammography while all the other structures (glandular, ductal and connective tissue) are radio-opaque. In most cases, the radio-opaque structures cannot be differentiated. Sometimes, lactiferous ducts can be identifified in their central, retroareolar region where they present a physiological dilatation called the lactiferous sinus and the Cooper ligaments can be seen in the anterior portion of the breast as fifine, opaque and curve lines attaching the breast parenchyma to the skin (fifigure 245).

30.4.2. Ultrasound

On ultrasound, the adipose tissue appears hypoechoic and the glandular tissue appears hyperechoic. Ducts are seen as round or tubular hypo or anechoic structures (fifigure 246). Fatty lobules interspersed with the glandular tissue should not be misinterpreted as pathological masses (fifigure 247).

The Abnormal Breast

Anca Ciurea, Ioana Ben

31.1. Semeiology of breast masses

The most important features in the differential diagnosis between benign and malignant breast masses are the shape and the margins.

Regular shape, round or oval, suggests a benign nature, while irregular shape (any other shape than round or oval) characterizes malignancies (fifigure 249).

The margins (or contour or outline) can be circumscribed, suggestive for benignity (see fifigure 249) or non circumscribed, suspicious. The non-circumscribed margins include the ill-defifined, lobulated and the spiculated contour (fifigure 250).

Besides the shape and margins, some other features specifific for each modality may suggest the benign or malignant nature of a breast mass. The presence or the absence of the associated features (skin retraction due to invasion, skin thickening due to edema, nipple retraction, architectural distortion, associated calcififications) is also helpful in the differential diagnosis of breast masses. ne

31.2. Imaging appearance of the most common breast pathologies

31.2.1. Cysts

Cysts are the most frequent benign masses and are part of fifibrocystic disease. Common in women between 25-45 years of age, they represent flfluid-fifilled cavities due to the accumulation of secretions in small ducts and lobules. They are frequently multiple and bilateral and have between a few millimeters in diameter up to more centimeters.

On mammography, they appear as round or oval nodular densities with circumscribed margins, impossible to be differentiated from other benign masses (e.g., fifibroadenomas) (fifigure 251).

Old cysts may sometimes present with rim calcififications (calcififications in the lesion wall) that suggest their benign nature.

On ultrasound, they appear as any other simple cysts, as anechoic, round or oval masses with posterior enhancement, well defifined by a thin echogenic wall (fifigure 252). Old or complicated cysts may present internal echoes of low density, mobile during examination (fifigure 253). 274 l VI. THE BREAST

MRI is not used to diagnose cysts, but they can be seen on images acquired during the MRI examination for other indications (e.g., local breast cancer staging). They present as regular and circumscribed masses in hypersignal T2 and hyposignal T1 (fifigure 254). On the dynamic images, they will show no uptake of the gadolinium-based contrast agent.

31.2.2. Fibroadenomas

Fibroadenomas are the most common solid breast tumors in adolescents and young women. They are benign biphasic tumors comprised of glandular epithelium and specialized interlobular stroma of the terminal ductal lobular unit (fifibro-epithelial tumors). They can be multiple or unique, uni or bilateral, and they suffer hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle, pregnancy or lactation.

On mammography, they present as oval, circumscribed densities (may have 2-3 discrete lobulations) (fifigure 255). Old, involuted fifibroadenomas may have characteristic “popcorn” calcififications (fifigure 256).

On ultrasound, fifibroadenomas are regular, well-defifined lesions, sometimes with some discrete lobulations. They have moderate hypoechoic echostructure compared with the fatty lobules and no posterior features. Typically, the orientation of fifibroadenomas is parallel to the skin (fifigure 257).

Doppler ultrasound presents a circumferential blood supply (fifigure 258) and the lesion is soft on elastography.

Old fifibroadenomas may present calcififications inside the mass (fifigure 259), case in which evaluation with mammography is mandatory to rule out malignant calcififications or may appear stiff on elastographic images.

31.2.3. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)

DCIS is a neoplastic proliferation of mammary ductal epithelial cells confifined within ducts and lobules, without invasion through the basement membrane into the surrounding stroma.

Most of the cases are diagnosed at screening mammography, and only a low proportion of the cases present as a palpable mass, nipple discharge or Paget disease of the nipple.

In up to 98% of the cases, DCIS presents on mammography with microcalcififications that are usually the only radiologic fifinding. The calcififications associated with DCIS are intraductal, with a linear and branching appearance or polymorphic and highly heterogeneous size, shape, and intensity (fifigure 261).

Less frequently, DCIS presents as a mass with or without calcififications or as architectural distortion.

On ultrasound, DCIS can be inapparent or present as a mass with calcififications or calcififications in the breast parenchyma (hyperechoic spots without shadowing) with no associated mass (fifigure 262). Even

31.2.4. Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC)

The invasive ductal carcinoma appears as a mass with malignant features (see above). More rarely, it may appear as architectural distortion without central mass.

31.2.5. Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC)

The ILC is a particular subtype of invasive breast carcinoma characterized by discohesive tumor cells arranged in single fifiles or as individual single cells.

On mammograms, it can be occult, can appear as a spiculated mass (just as the IDC), architectural distortion as an asymmetric focal density (fifigure 264). The association of malignant calcififications is unusual in ILC. distortion on the 3D mammogram in MLO (a) and
